cards.explanation: The answer is twelve stones. The LORD tells Joshua to have the men take up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, carry them along, and set them down where they spend the night. Joshua's own words are that each man takes a stone upon his shoulder. I stamp cookies for a living, friends, so my shoulders just filed a complaint.

The answer is True. The LORD says to take the stones "…from the middle of the Jordan where the priests were standing…" (Joshua 4:3). So these aren't just any rocks from along the riverbank, friends. They come from that exact place, and that matters later in the passage.

The answer is their children. Joshua says that in the future, when your children ask, 'What do these stones mean to you?' there will be an answer waiting (Joshua 4:6). Twelve big stones sitting there will get a kid's attention. Kids ask questions, friends, and these stones are built to start the conversation.

The answer is False. Joshua says to tell them, "The waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD." (Joshua 4:7). Nobody's bragging about a victory here, friends. The stones point to the river and the ark, and that's the whole answer.

The answer is memorial. Joshua says, "Therefore these stones will be a memorial to the Israelites forever." (Joshua 4:7). A memorial helps people remember, and these stones remember the day the waters of the Jordan were cut off. Big stones are good at that, friends, because they're hard to lose.

The answer is the camp. The Israelites took up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, "and they carried them to the camp, where they set them down." (Joshua 4:8). That matches what the LORD told Joshua. Twelve stones, one per tribe, all hauled to the camp.

The answer is right in the middle of the Jordan. Joshua set up twelve stones "…in the place where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood." (Joshua 4:9). So there's a second set of stones, friends, and this set sits where the priests stood. And the writer says the stones are there to this day.

The answer is False. The priests who carried the ark "…remained standing in the middle of the Jordan…" until the people had completed everything the LORD had commanded Joshua to tell them (Joshua 4:10). They don't wait on the far bank, friends. They stay planted in the middle of the river.

The answer is that they cross over while the people watch. After everyone had finished crossing, "…the priests with the ark of the LORD crossed in the sight of the people." (Joshua 4:11). The people go first, and the priests with the ark come last. Everybody gets to watch them make it over.

The answer is armed for battle. These tribes crossed over before the Israelites, "…armed for battle as Moses had instructed them." (Joshua 4:12). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua. So these tribes are walking in with weapons, friends, and they're doing it the way Moses told them.

The answer is that He exalts him. "On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel…" (Joshua 4:14). The text adds that they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses. I think that's quite a day for Joshua, with the whole nation watching. Nobody had to puff him up, friends.

The answer is Moses. The verse says Israel revered Joshua "…all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses." (Joshua 4:14). Moses is the one who had directed Joshua. So Joshua gets the same kind of respect Moses had.

The answer is that the waters return and overflow the banks. When the priests' feet touched the dry land, "…the waters of the Jordan returned to their course and overflowed all the banks as before." (Joshua 4:18). The river that had been cut off is back to normal, banks and all. And the people had already crossed on dry ground.

The answer is Gilgal. The people went up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped "…at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho." (Joshua 4:19). It's also where Joshua sets up the twelve stones. So Gilgal is the stones' new home, friends.

The answer is True. "And there at Gilgal Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan." (Joshua 4:20). These are the stones the twelve men carried out of the river. They came from the Jordan and now stand at Gilgal. I know a little about getting moved to a new spot, friends, and a new place beats the back of a junk drawer every time.

The answer is dry. Joshua says to tell them, "Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground." (Joshua 4:22). He goes on to say the LORD dried up the Jordan "…just as He did to the Red Sea…" (Joshua 4:23). Dry ground in the middle of a river, friends. I'd have checked it twice.

The answer is False. Joshua says the LORD dried up the Jordan "…just as He did to the Red Sea, which He dried up before us until we had crossed over." (Joshua 4:23). The comparison is the Red Sea, friends. Two crossings, and in both the water was dried up before Israel.

The answer is so all peoples know His hand is mighty. Joshua says the LORD did it "…so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty…" (Joshua 4:24). So this crossing isn't only for Israel to see, friends. It's meant for all the peoples of the earth.
The answer is True. Joshua says the LORD did it "…so that you may always fear the LORD your God." (Joshua 4:24). Joshua gives this reason for Israel itself, friends, and it's meant to last always.

The answer is that their hearts melt with fear. When the Amorite and Canaanite kings heard how the LORD had dried up the Jordan, "…their hearts melted and their spirits failed for fear of the Israelites." (Joshua 5:1). That's quite a reaction to a river story, friends. The news about the Jordan reached them.
